findings.text: Within the first paragraph, a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The 'what' and 'why' are covered right away.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The header links straight to a concrete Next steps section with a clone command, prerequisites, `./setup.sh` and a sample `athena ask "add a changelog"` request. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself

findings.text: The title is about firstmate, not Athena, and almost all of the page is a detailed study of firstmate's internals (states, transitions, 45 claims). Someone who came to learn about Athena has to work out that the study is a sample of Athena's output, not the main subject.
findings.source: Athena explains how firstmate handles work

findings.text: The opening promises that work can be traced to the models, the cost and the verdict, but the page never shows which models made or checked this study, or what it cost. The sample doesn't demonstrate the features the opening sells.
findings.source: It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This link sits in the header with no explanation of who the owner is. A newcomer may think it is meant for them, or not know what 'proposals' means here.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The prerequisites are concrete. But Athena is described as written in Rust and no Rust toolchain is listed, so a reader can't tell whether `setup.sh` installs one. The page also doesn't say which operating systems are supported.
findings.source: Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code).

findings.text: Defining terms like captain, yolo, green and red before they are used, and again in the Glossary, makes the dense firstmate material readable for a stranger. The cards still pile up many qualifiers in one summary, though, for example t8 and t10.

The Limits section is open about what the study did not check. That builds trust, but it also tells a newcomer that this sample of Athena's work needed a second pass and was never confirmed by running anything.
findings.source: f3 ... A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths ... none was run, so no run confirmed that a script behaves as its header says.

findings.text: The About section points to a `studies/` folder without a link or the name of its repository, so a newcomer can't easily find the source data.
findings.source: This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from.
